evidence.title: Board meeting summary — 2026-02-01
evidence.text: # Board meeting summary — 2026-02-01 Just finishing up the notes from our check-in. The main deck is linked over in [[Board Decks]], but I wanted to drop a quick summary here for the team since everyone's been heads-down on [[Pulse]] infrastructure lately. The big headline from the [[2026-02-01]] board meeting is that Lumen Labs reported $2.1M ARR at the 2026-02-01 board meeting, up from $1.4M the prior quarter. Everyone was pretty stoked about that trajectory, especially given the infrastructure scaling pains we pushed through over the last few months. A lot of the credit goes to the recent push on retention and the new tier rollouts we discussed back in [[Q4 Planning]]. We also touched on upcoming roadmap items for [[Aurora migration]] and how that ties into enterprise readiness, but the financial update was definitely the anchor of the session. Let's make sure we share this milestone in the general chat tomorrow so everyone sees the momentum we're carrying into the next sprint.

evidence.title: Weekly eng sync — 2026-02-05
evidence.text: # Weekly eng sync — 2026-02-05 Had our usual Thursday catch-up today. Everyone's mostly heads-down on their current iteration cycles. The frontend crew mentioned they're still poking around at some bundle size optimization stuff [[Aurora migration]]. Nothing major broke this week, which is always nice. Sarah's group [[Helios]] is continuing their work on cleaning up some legacy components in the event ingestion pipeline, mostly just chipping away at tech debt that’s been sitting there for a while. We talked briefly about the upcoming office snack restock—consensus is we need more sparkling water and fewer fruit snacks that nobody touches. After that, we spent a few minutes reviewing the general load balancer charts. Everything looked flat and green over the last seven days, so no fires to put out there. Quick reminder to everyone: remember to update your local dependencies before running the integration test suites, otherwise you'll hit weird caching issues. That was pretty much it. Short and sweet. Back to the code.

evidence.title: Decision record: usage-based pricing
evidence.text: # Decision record: usage-based pricing We had the sync this morning to finally wrap up the endless billing discussions and get everyone aligned on the shift away from the old [[Pulse pricing (2025 launch)]] model. It's been clear for a while that charging by the seat just doesn't align with how customers actually use the platform, especially as teams share logins or automate testing pipelines. After reviewing the final numbers and the [[Aurora migration]] timeline, usage-based pricing was approved on 2026-01-14 to replace seat-based pricing, effective 2026-04-01. Under the new model, customers will be billed per session recorded. This means our billing will directly scale with the volume of data they send to [[Pulse]], which better matches our underlying infrastructure costs and provides a much cleaner entry point for smaller teams who were previously blocked by minimum seat tiers. The product and engineering squads need to make sure the metering infrastructure is fully baked before the April rollout, and customer success should start drafting communication touchpoints for our existing accounts next week. We'll also need to update the [[Helios]] integration docs so the new telemetry metrics map correctly to the usage counters.

evidence.title: Infra review — 2026-01-20
evidence.text: # Infra review — 2026-01-20 Good turnout today for the sync. Mostly went over the usual [[Pulse]] backend metrics, but we spent a good chunk of time diving into the current database setup and why everyone keeps getting paged at 3 AM. The main pain point continues to be manual maintenance on the self-hosted instances. Between disk space alerts, routine patching, and replication lag [[Helios]], the team is spending way too much time babysitting infrastructure instead of shipping features for [[Pulse]]. After looking at a few options, the team decided at the 2026-01-20 infra review to migrate the primary Postgres database from self-hosted to a managed provider (Aurora), to reduce on-call burden. Moving to Aurora should take a massive weight off the [[Aurora migration]] project backlog. We'll get automated backups, easier scaling, and—most importantly—fewer middle-of-the-night alerts for the engineering rotation. Will spin up a staging cluster next week to benchmark the read/write performance against our current setup. If the numbers look good, we'll draft a proper cutover timeline and share it with the rest of the crew.

evidence.title: Product roadmap — H1 2026
evidence.text: # Product roadmap — H1 2026 Here is our working outline for the upcoming half. The general focus for H1 2026 is on stabilizing our core data ingestion pipelines and improving overall dashboard responsiveness for larger teams. We want to make sure the core experience feels snappy before rolling out any major visual overhauls. A lot of this ties back to the ongoing work in [[Aurora migration]], which should give us the database performance headroom we need to support heavier query loads. On the feature side, we are currently tracking a few key initiatives. First, we need to finalize the scope for [[Helios]] so the design team can start exploring mockups by late Q1. Second, engineering has [[API v3]] on the docket as a background effort, primarily focused on cleaning up deprecated endpoints and improving developer documentation rather than rewriting the whole contract overnight. Customer feedback from the last few user interviews highlighted that session filtering still feels a bit clunky when dealing with high-volume noise. We should schedule a quick sync with support next week to pull some recent examples of those failing queries so the frontend squad has realistic test cases. As usual, this is a living document and will likely shift a bit once we lock in engineering capacity during our next planning retro. Feel free to drop comments or questions directly in the thread.

evidence.title: Marketing campaign retro — Q4 2025
evidence.text: # Marketing campaign retro — Q4 2025 Overall, the Q4 push felt a lot smoother than our mid-year [[lead generation]] sprint, mostly because we actually had [[design assets]] ready before the first batch of ads went live. We tried out three different [[audience segments]] for the new [[explainer video]], and the middle-tier developer persona definitely outperformed the enterprise-focused one. That said, coordination between [[content production]] and the [[growth team]] could still use some work. Halfway through November, we noticed a few typos in the primary landing page copy that had been sitting there for over a week. Nobody flagged it because everyone assumed someone else owned the [[copywriting review]] loop. For the next [[budget cycle]], we should probably allocate more resources toward [[community events]] rather than purely pouring money into paid search. The conversion rates from the [[developer meetup]] sponsorships were surprisingly solid, even if they are harder to attribute directly in [[analytics dashboards]]. Let’s make sure we schedule a proper [[strategy sync]] before diving into any new [[collaboration tools]] or agency pitches for the upcoming quarter.

evidence.title: Postmortem: Northwind missing session replays
evidence.text: # Postmortem: Northwind missing session replays We spent the morning digging into the ticket [[Northwind Retail]] opened about gaps in their [[session replay]] data. Things looked fine on our end during initial checks, but once we pulled the raw edge logs, the picture cleared up. It turns out that Northwind Retail's missing session replays were caused by an ad-blocker false-positive flagging Pulse's mobile SDK script as a tracker. Popular consumer list blocklists had recently updated their heuristic rules, which unfortunately caught our ingestion endpoint in the crossfire for a subset of end-users running strict browser extensions or device-level protection. The good news is that no data was actually corrupted or dropped on our servers; the payloads simply never made it out of the clients' devices. To prevent this from biting us again with other enterprise accounts, we need to fast-track our [[SDK proxy]] routing options and review our [[domain masking]] recommendations. I've updated [[Runbook - Adblock Mitigation]] with the specific signature patterns we found in this case so support can spot it faster next time. Let's sync during tomorrow's [[engineering standup]] to prioritize the domain fallback work.

evidence.title: Security incident log — stored XSS (2026-02-25)
evidence.text: # Security incident log — stored XSS (2026-02-25) Quick follow-up on the bug bounty submission from yesterday regarding the session replay renderer. The security researcher who reported the stored XSS vulnerability was paid a $1,500 bounty, approved by Ravi Anand. We had a brief sync with the [[Core Engineering]] team to ensure the payload sanitation was rolled out properly across all active [[Pulse]] endpoints. Everything looks stable now, and the automated regression suite passed without any issues. Just dropping this here for the [[Security Audits]] vault so we have a clean paper trail for the upcoming compliance check. Ravi signed off on the payout this morning through [[Finance]], so the ticket is fully closed out on our end.
